questions.q: Let the tangent at any point $P$ on a curve passing through the points $\left(1, 1\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{1}{10}, 100\right)$, intersect positive $x$-axis and $y$-axis at the points $A$ and $B$ respectively. If $PA: PB = 1: k$ and $y = y\left(x\right)$ is the solution of the differential equation $e\dfrac{dy}{dx} = kx + \dfrac{k}{2}, y\left(0\right) = k$, then $4y\left(1\right) - 5{log}_{e}3$ is equal to _______________
questions.question: Let the tangent at any point $P$ on a curve passing through the points $\left(1, 1\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{1}{10}, 100\right)$, intersect positive $x$-axis and $y$-axis at the points $A$ and $B$ respectively. If $PA: PB = 1: k$ and $y = y\left(x\right)$ is the solution of the differential equation $e\dfrac{dy}{dx} = kx + \dfrac{k}{2}, y\left(0\right) = k$, then $4y\left(1\right) - 5{log}_{e}3$ is equal to _______________
questions.solution:
Given,

The tangent at any point $P$ on a curve passing through the points $\left(1, 1\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{1}{10}, 100\right)$, intersect positive $x$-axis and $y$-axis at the points $A$ and $B$ respectively,

And $PA: PB = 1: k$ and $y = y\left(x\right)$ is the solution of the differential equation $e\dfrac{dy}{dx} = kx + \dfrac{k}{2}, y\left(0\right) = k$,

Now on plotting the diagram we get,

Equation of tangent at $P\left(x, y\right)$ is :

$Y - y = \dfrac{dy}{dx}\left(X - x\right)$

Coordinate of $A = \left(x - y\dfrac{dx}{dy}, 0\right)$

Coordinate of $B = \left(0, y - x\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)$

$∴ \left(x, y\right) = \left(\dfrac{kx - ky\dfrac{dx}{dy}}{k + 1}, \dfrac{y - x\dfrac{dy}{dx}}{k + 1}\right)$

So, $y = \dfrac{y - x\dfrac{dy}{dx}}{k + 1}$

$⇒ y\left(k + 1\right) = y - x\dfrac{dy}{dx}$

$⇒ ky = - x\dfrac{dy}{dx}$

$⇒ k\dfrac{dx}{x} = - \dfrac{dy}{y}$

Now integrating both side, we get

$kln | x | + ln | y | = lnC . . . . . . \left(i\right)$

Now given equation $\left(i\right)$ passes through $\left(1, 1\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{1}{10}, 100\right)$

So, $C = 1$ and $k = 2$

Now putting the value of $k$, we get

$e\dfrac{dy}{dx} = kx + \dfrac{k}{2}$

$⇒ e\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2x + 1\left\{\text{as}k = 2\right\}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = ln\left(2x + 1\right)$

Integrating the above equation we get,

$y = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(2x + 1\right)\left(ln\left|2x + 1\right| - 1\right) + C$

And the above equation passes through $\left(0, 2\right)$

$⇒ C = \dfrac{5}{2}$

So, $2y = \left(2x + 1\right)\left(ln\left|2x + 1\right| - 1\right) + 5$

$⇒ 2y\left(1\right) = 3\left(ln3 - 1\right) + 5$

$⇒ 2y\left(1\right) = 3ln\left(3\right) + 2$

Hence, $4y\left(1\right) - 5{log}_{e}3 = 2\left[3ln3 + 2\right] - 5ln3$

$⇒ 4y\left(1\right) - 5{log}_{e}3 = 6ln3 + 4 - 5ln3$

$⇒ 4y\left(1\right) - 5{log}_{e}3 = 4 + ln3 \approx 5$

Note: This question was bonus in Jee Mains 2023 April session.

questions.question: Let a curve $y = y\left(x\right)$ pass through the point $\left(3, 3\right)$ and the area of the region under this curve, above the $x$-axis and between the abscissae $3$ and $x\left(> 3\right)$ be $\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)3$. If this curve also passes through the point $\left(\alpha, 6\sqrt{10}\right)$ in the first quadrant, then $\alpha$ is equal to _______.
questions.solution:
Given, the area of the region under this curve, above the $x$-axis and between the abscissae $3$ and $x\left(> 3\right)$ be $\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)3$

So, ${∫}_{3}^{x}y d x = \left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)3$

$⇒ {x}^{3}{∫}_{3}^{x}y d x = {y}^{3}$

Now differentiating both side w.r.t $x$, we get

$⇒ {x}^{3}y + 3{x}^{2}\dfrac{y3}{x3} = 3{y}^{2}\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ $\left\{\text{as given}{∫}_{3}^{x}y d x = \left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)3\right\}$

$⇒ {x}^{4} + 3{y}^{2} = 3yx\dfrac{dy}{dx}$

$⇒ 3xy\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3{y}^{2} + {x}^{4}$

Now put ${y}^{2} = t, y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{dt}{dx}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dt}{dx} - \dfrac{2}{x}t = \dfrac{2}{3}{x}^{3}$

Now $IF = {e}^{∫ - \dfrac{2}{x}dx} = \dfrac{1}{x2}$

So, solution is given by

$t \times IF = ∫ \dfrac{2}{3}{x}^{3} \times IF$

$⇒ \dfrac{t}{x2} = \dfrac{x2}{3} + C$

Now given curve passes through $\left(3, 3\right)$ so $C = - 2$

$⇒ \dfrac{y2}{x2} = \dfrac{x2}{3} - 2$

So the equation of curve is $3{y}^{2} = {x}^{4} - 6{x}^{2}$

Now curve also passes through $\left(\alpha, 6\sqrt{10}\right)$

So, ${α}^{4} - 6{α}^{2} = 1080$

$⇒ \alpha = 6$

questions.question: Let $f: \mathbf{R} \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ be a thrice differentiable odd function satisfying $f^{\prime}(\mathrm{x}) \geq 0, f^{\prime}(\mathrm{x})=f(\mathrm{x}), f(0)=0, f^{\prime}(0)=3$. Then $9 f\left(\log _{\mathrm{c}} 3\right)$ is equal to _______.

$\mathrm{f}(0)=0, \mathrm{f}^{\prime}(0)=3 \quad \Rightarrow \mathrm{C}^{\prime}=9$
$\therefore\left(\mathrm{f}^{\prime}(\mathrm{x})\right)^2=(\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}))^2+9$
$\mathrm{f}^{\prime}(\mathrm{x})=\sqrt{(\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}))^2+9} \quad \because \mathrm{f}^{\prime}(\mathrm{x}) \geq 0$
$\int \frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{y}^2+9}}=\int \mathrm{dx} \Rightarrow \ln \left|\mathrm{y}+\sqrt{\mathrm{y}^2+9}\right|=\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{C}$
$\Rightarrow \mathrm{f}(0)=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{C}=\ln 3$
$\Rightarrow \mathrm{y}+\sqrt{\mathrm{y}^2+9}=3 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}$
at $x=\ln 3 ; y=4$
$\therefore 9 \mathrm{f}(\ln 3)=36$

questions.question: If the solution of the differential equation $( 2x + 3y - 2 ) dx + ( 4x + 6y - 7 ) dy = 0, y ( 0 ) = 3$, is $\alphax + \betay + 3{log}_{e} | 2x + 3y - \gamma | = 6$, then $\alpha + 2\beta + 3\gamma$ is equal to ______.
questions.solution:
Given: $( 2x + 3y - 2 ) dx + ( 4x + 6y - 7 ) dy = 0$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = - \left(2x + 3y - 2\right)\left(4x + 6y - 7\right) . . . \left(i\right)$

Let, $2x + 3y - 2 = t$

$⇒ 2 + 3\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dt}{dx} . . . \left(ii\right)$

Also, $4x + 6y - 4 = 2t$

$⇒ 4x + 6y - 7 = 2t - 3 . . . \left(iii\right)$

Using $\left(i\right), \left(ii\right)\text{and}\left(iii\right)$,

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{dt}{dx} - 2\right) = \dfrac{- t}{2t - 3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dt}{dx} - 2 = \dfrac{- 3t}{2t - 3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dt}{dx} = \dfrac{- 3t}{2t - 3} + 2$

$⇒ \dfrac{dt}{dx} = \dfrac{- 3t + 4t - 6}{2t - 3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dt}{dx} = \dfrac{t - 6}{2t - 3}$

$⇒ ∫ \dfrac{2t - 3}{t - 6}dt = ∫ dx$

$⇒ ∫ \left(\dfrac{2t - 12}{t - 6} + \dfrac{9}{t - 6}\right) \cdot dt = x + c$

$⇒ 2t + 9log ( t - 6 ) = x + c$

$⇒ 2 ( 2x + 3y - 2 ) + 9log ( 2x + 3y - 8 ) = x + c . . . \left(iv\right)$

It is given that $y ( 0 ) = 3$.

$⇒ 2 ( 0 + 9 - 2 ) + 9log ( 0 + 9 - 8 ) = 0 + c$

$⇒ 14 + 9log ( 1 ) = c$

$⇒ c = 14$

Using $\left(iv\right)$,

$⇒ 4x + 6y - 4 + 9log ( 2x + 3y - 8 ) = x + 14$

$⇒ 3x + 6y + 9log ( 2x + 3y - 8 ) = 18$

$⇒ x + 2y + 3log ( 2x + 3y - 8 ) = 6$

Comparing with $\alphax + \betay + 3{log}_{e} | 2x + 3y - \gamma | = 6$.

$⇒ \alpha = 1, \beta = 2, \gamma = 8$

$⇒ \alpha + 2\beta + 3\gamma = 1 + 4 + 24$

$⇒ \alpha + 2\beta + 3\gamma = 29$

Putting $x = 0 ⇒ 2 = - B ⇒ B = - 2$

$⇒ k = ln2$

questions.solution:
The given differential equation can be written as:

$(1 + \sin x)dy + (y+1)\cos x dx = 0$

$d((y+1)(1 + \sin x)) = 0$

Integrating both sides:

$(y+1)(1 + \sin x) = C$

Given $y(0) = 0$, substituting $x = 0$ and $y = 0$:

$(0+1)(1 + \sin 0) = C \Rightarrow C = 1$

The equation of the curve is $(y+1)(1 + \sin x) = 1$

Since the curve passes through $\left(\alpha, \dfrac{-1}{2}\right)$, substituting $x = \alpha$ and $y = \dfrac{-1}{2}$:

$\left(\dfrac{-1}{2} + 1\right)(1 + \sin \alpha) = 1$

$\dfrac{1}{2}(1 + \sin \alpha) = 1$

$1 + \sin \alpha = 2$

$\sin \alpha = 1$

$\alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

questions.question: Let $f$ be a twice differentiable function such that $f(x)=\int_{0}^{x}\tan(t-x)dt-\int_{0}^{x}f(t)\tan t\,dt$, $x \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. Then $f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+12f'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)+f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ is equal to ______
questions.solution:
Given the function:

$f(x) = \int_{0}^{x} \tan(t-x) dt - \int_{0}^{x} f(t) \tan t \, dt$

First, we simplify the first integral. Let $u = x - t$, then $du = -dt$. When $t = 0$, $u = x$; when $t = x$, $u = 0$.

$\int_{0}^{x} \tan(t-x) dt = \int_{x}^{0} \tan(-u) (-du) = \int_{x}^{0} \tan u \, du = -\int_{0}^{x} \tan u \, du = -[\ln(\sec u)]_{0}^{x} = -\ln(\sec x) = \ln(\cos x)$

So, the equation becomes:

$f(x) = \ln(\cos x) - \int_{0}^{x} f(t) \tan t \, dt$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ using the Leibniz rule:

$f'(x) = \dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x} - f(x) \tan x$

$f'(x) + f(x) \tan x = -\tan x$

This is a linear first-order differential equation. The integrating factor (IF) is:

$\text{IF} = e^{\int \tan x \, dx} = e^{\ln(\sec x)} = \sec x$

Multiplying the differential equation by $\sec x$:

$f'(x) \sec x + f(x) \sec x \tan x = -\sec x \tan x$

$\dfrac{d}{dx} (f(x) \sec x) = -\sec x \tan x$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$:

$f(x) \sec x = -\sec x + C$

To find $C$, we use the initial condition. From $f(x) = \ln(\cos x) - \int_{0}^{x} f(t) \tan t \, dt$, substituting $x = 0$ gives $f(0) = \ln(1) - 0 = 0$.

$0 \cdot \sec 0 = -\sec 0 + C \Rightarrow 0 = -1 + C \Rightarrow C = 1$

Thus, $f(x) \sec x = 1 - \sec x$

$f(x) = \cos x - 1$

Now, we find the required derivatives:

$f'(x) = -\sin x$

$f''(x) = -\cos x$

Evaluating these at the given points:

$f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) - 1 = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 1$

$f'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

Finally, substituting these values into the required expression:

$f''\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) + 12f'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) + f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 12\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 1\right)$

$= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 6 + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 1 = 5$

Answer: $5$

questions.solution:

Using $f(0) = 1$ and $f'(0) = 2$: $A = 1$, $k = 2$

$g'(x) > 0$ when $\frac{1-x}{x} > 0$, i.e., $0 < x < 1$
$(\alpha, \beta) = (0, 1)$

questions.question: Let $y = y\left(x\right)$ be the solution of the differential equation $xtan\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)dy = \left(ytan\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) - x\right)dx$, $- 1 \le x \le 1, y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{π}{6} .$ Then the area of the region bounded by the curves $x = 0, x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $y = y\left(x\right)$ in the upper half plane is:
questions.solution:
We have,

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x\left(\dfrac{y}{x} \cdot tan\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) - 1\right)}{xtan\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)}$
$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{y}{x} - cot\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)$

Put $y = vx$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x\left(\dfrac{dv}{dx}\right)$

Now, we get

$v + x\left(\dfrac{dv}{dx}\right) = v - cotv$

$⇒ ∫ tanvdv = - ∫ \dfrac{dx}{x}$

$⇒ ln\left|secv\right| = - ln\left|x\right| + c$

$⇒ ln\left|sec\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)\right| = - ln\left|x\right| + c$

$⇒ ln\left|sec\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)\right| + ln\left|x\right| = c$

Now, $y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{π}{6}$, then

$ln\left|sec\left(\dfrac{π}{3}\right)\right| + ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = c$

$⇒ ln2 + ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = c$

$⇒ ln2 - ln2 = c$

$⇒ c = 0$

Hence,

$∴ sec\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) = \dfrac{1}{x}$

$⇒ cos\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) = x$

$⇒ y = x{cos}^{- 1}\left(x\right)$

So, required bounded area

$= {∫}_{0}^{1\sqrt{2}}\left(\mathop{{cos}^{- 1}x ⏟}_{I}\right)\mathop{x}_{II}dx$

$= {{cos}^{- 1}x \cdot \left(\dfrac{x2}{2}\right)}_{0}^{1\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{2}{∫}_{0}^{1\sqrt{2}}\left(\dfrac{x2}{1 - {x}^{2}}\right)dx$

$= \dfrac{π}{16} - \dfrac{1}{2}{∫}_{0}^{1\sqrt{2}}\left(\dfrac{1 - {x}^{2} - 1}{1 - {x}^{2}}\right)dx$

$= \dfrac{π}{16} - \dfrac{1}{2}{∫}_{0}^{1\sqrt{2}}\left(\sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{1 - {x}^{2}}\right)dx$

$= \dfrac{π}{16} - \dfrac{1}{2}{\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{2}{sin}^{- 1}x - {sin}^{- 1}x}_{0}^{1\sqrt{2}}$

$= \dfrac{π}{16} - \dfrac{1}{2}{\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{1 - {x}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{2}{sin}^{- 1}x}_{0}^{1\sqrt{2}}$

$= \dfrac{π}{16} - \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{π}{8}\right]$

$= \left(\dfrac{\pi - 1}{8}\right)$ sq. units

questions.solution:
Given ${y}^{2}dx + \left({x}^{2} - xy + {y}^{2}\right)dy = 0$

$⇒ \dfrac{dx}{dy} = - \left({x}^{2} - xy + {y}^{2}\right){y}^{2} . . . \left(i\right)$

Now let $x = vy$ $⇒ v + y\dfrac{dv}{dy} = \dfrac{dx}{dy}$

Now putting in equation $\left(i\right)$ we get

$⇒ v + y\dfrac{dv}{dy} = - \left({v}^{2} - v + 1\right)$

$⇒ y\dfrac{dv}{dy} = - {v}^{2} - 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{- dv}{1 + {v}^{2}} = \dfrac{dy}{y}$

Now Integrating Both side

$⇒ - ∫ \dfrac{dy}{1 + {v}^{2}} = ∫ \dfrac{dy}{y}$

$⇒ - {tan}^{- 1}v = log\left|y\right| + c$ $⇒ - {tan}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) = log\left|y\right| + c$

Also this curve passes through $\left(1, 1\right)$

$⇒ {tan}^{- 1}1 = log\left|1\right| + c$ $⇒ c = - \dfrac{π}{4}$

$⇒ - {tan}^{- 1}\dfrac{x}{y} = log\left|y\right| - \dfrac{π}{4}$

Now putting $y = \sqrt{3}x$ and $x = \alpha$ we get

$= - {tan}^{- 1}\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{3}x} = log\left|\sqrt{3}\alpha\right| - \dfrac{π}{4}$ $= - {tan}^{- 1}\dfrac{1}{3} = log\left(\sqrt{3}\alpha\right) - \dfrac{π}{4}$

$= - \dfrac{π}{6} + \dfrac{π}{4} = log\left|\sqrt{3}\alpha\right|$

$⇒ log\left|\sqrt{3}\alpha\right| = \dfrac{π}{12}$

Let $\dfrac{y}{x} = t$

$⇒ y = xt$

$⇒ xt\dfrac{dt}{dx} = \dfrac{ϕ\left({t}^{2}\right)}{ϕ ' \left({t}^{2}\right)}$

$⇒ \dfrac{t \cdot {ϕ}^{'}\left({t}^{2}\right)}{ϕ\left({t}^{2}\right)}dt = \dfrac{1}{x}dx$

$∫ \dfrac{t \cdot {ϕ}^{'}\left({t}^{2}\right)}{ϕ\left({t}^{2}\right)}dt = ∫ \dfrac{1}{x}dx$

Let $ϕ\left({t}^{2}\right) = p$

$⇒ {ϕ}^{'}\left({t}^{2}\right) . 2t = dp$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2} ∫ \dfrac{1}{p}dp = ∫ \dfrac{1}{x}dx$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}lnp = lnx + C$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}lnϕ\left({t}^{2}\right) = lnx + C$

$⇒$$ln\left(ϕ\left(\dfrac{y2}{x2}\right)\right) = ln{x}^{2} + ln\left(ϕ\left(1\right)\right)$

If $x = 2$ then

questions.question: If the solution curve of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x + y - 2}{x - y}$ passes through the point $\left(2, 1\right)$ and $\left(k + 1, 2\right), k > 0$, then
questions.solution:
Given,

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x + y - 2}{x - y} = \dfrac{\left(x - 1\right) + \left(y - 1\right)}{\left(x - 1\right) - \left(y - 1\right)}$

Now let $x - 1 = X, y - 1 = Y$

So, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{X + Y}{X - Y} . . . . . . . . \left(1\right)$

Now let $Y = VX\dfrac{dY}{dX} = V + X\dfrac{dV}{dX}$

Putting the value in equation $\left(1\right)$ we get,

$V + X\dfrac{dV}{dX} = \dfrac{1 + V}{1 - V}$

$⇒ X\dfrac{dV}{dX} = \dfrac{{V}^{2} + 1}{1 - V}$

$⇒ ∫ \dfrac{1 - V}{1 + {V}^{2}}dV = ∫ \dfrac{dX}{X}$

$⇒ ∫ \dfrac{dV}{1 + {V}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{2} ∫ \dfrac{2VdV}{1 + {V}^{2}} = ∫ \dfrac{dX}{X}$

$⇒ {tan}^{- 1}V - \dfrac{1}{2}ln\left(1 + {V}^{2}\right) = lnX + c$

$⇒ {tan}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{Y}{X}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}ln\left(1 + \dfrac{Y2}{X2}\right) = ln\left(X\right) + c$

$⇒ {tan}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{y - 1}{x - 1}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}ln\left(1 + \dfrac{\left(y - 1\right)2}{\left(x - 1\right)2}\right) = ln\left(x - 1\right) + c$

Now given curve passes through $\left(2, 1\right)$

So, $0 - \dfrac{1}{2}ln1 = ln1 + c ⇒ c = 0$

Now given curve also passes through $\left(k + 1, 2\right)$

So, ${tan}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{k}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2} In \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{k2}\right) = lnk$

$⇒ 2{tan}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{k}\right) = In \left(\dfrac{1 + {k}^{2}}{k2}\right) + 2lnk$

$⇒ 2{tan}^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{k}\right) = In \left(1 + {k}^{2}\right)$

If the solution curve $y=f(x)$ of the differential equation
$\left(x^{2}-4\right) y^{\prime}-2 x y+2 x\left(4-x^{2}\right)^{2}=0, x>2$,
passes through the point $(3,15)$, then the local maximum value of $f$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
Rewriting: $\frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{2x}{x^2-4}y = -2x(x^2-4)$.
IF $= e^{-\int \frac{2x}{x^2-4}dx} = \frac{1}{x^2-4}$.
$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{y}{x^2-4}\right) = -2x \Rightarrow \frac{y}{x^2-4} = -x^2 + C$.
$y = (x^2-4)(C-x^2)$. At $(3,15)$: $15 = 5(C-9) \Rightarrow C = 12$.
$y = (x^2-4)(12-x^2)$.
$y' = 4x(8-x^2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2\sqrt{2}$ (for $x > 2$).
$y'' = 32 - 12x^2 = -64 < 0$ at $x = 2\sqrt{2}$, confirming local maximum.
$f(2\sqrt{2}) = (8-4)(12-8) = 16$.

questions.question: Let $y = y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $(\tan x)^{1/2}\,dy = (\sec^3 x - (\tan x)^{3/2} y)\,dx$, $0 < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{6\sqrt{2}}{5}$. If $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{4}{5}\alpha$, then $\alpha^4$ equals _______.
questions.solution:
The given differential equation can be rewritten as:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} + (\tan x)y = \dfrac{\sec^3 x}{(\tan x)^{1/2}}$

This is a linear differential equation of the form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$.

Integrating Factor (IF) = $e^{\int \tan x \, dx} = e^{\ln(\sec x)} = \sec x$

Multiplying both sides by the IF and integrating, we get:

$y \sec x = \int \dfrac{\sec^4 x}{(\tan x)^{1/2}} \, dx + C$

$y \sec x = \int \dfrac{(1 + \tan^2 x)\sec^2 x}{(\tan x)^{1/2}} \, dx + C$

Let $\tan x = t$, then $\sec^2 x \, dx = dt$.

$y \sec x = \int \dfrac{1 + t^2}{t^{1/2}} \, dt + C$

$y \sec x = \int (t^{-1/2} + t^{3/2}) \, dt + C$

$y \sec x = 2t^{1/2} + \dfrac{2}{5}t^{5/2} + C$

$y \sec x = 2(\tan x)^{1/2} + \dfrac{2}{5}(\tan x)^{5/2} + C$

Given $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{6\sqrt{2}}{5}$, substituting $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:

$\dfrac{6\sqrt{2}}{5} \cdot \sqrt{2} = 2(1)^{1/2} + \dfrac{2}{5}(1)^{5/2} + C$

$\dfrac{12}{5} = 2 + \dfrac{2}{5} + C \Rightarrow C = 0$

The solution is $y \sec x = 2(\tan x)^{1/2} + \dfrac{2}{5}(\tan x)^{5/2}$.

Substituting $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$:

$y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \cdot 2 = 2(\sqrt{3})^{1/2} + \dfrac{2}{5}(\sqrt{3})^{5/2}$

$y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 3^{1/4} + \dfrac{1}{5} \cdot 3^{5/4} = 3^{1/4}\left(1 + \dfrac{3}{5}\right) = \dfrac{8}{5} \cdot 3^{1/4}$

Given $y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{4}{5}\alpha$, we have:

$\dfrac{4}{5}\alpha = \dfrac{8}{5} \cdot 3^{1/4} \Rightarrow \alpha = 2 \cdot 3^{1/4}$

Therefore, $\alpha^4 = (2 \cdot 3^{1/4})^4 = 16 \cdot 3 = 48$

Answer: $48$

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dy + \left(y\sqrt{1-x^2} - x\cos^{-1}x\right)dx = 0$, $x \in (0, 1)$, $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 1^-} y(x) = 1$. Then $y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ equals:
questions.solution:
The given differential equation is:

$x\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dy + \left(y\sqrt{1-x^2} - x\cos^{-1}x\right)dx = 0$

Rearranging the terms, we get:

$x\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dy + y\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx = x\cos^{-1}x\,dx$

Dividing the entire equation by $\sqrt{1-x^2}$:

$x\,dy + y\,dx = \dfrac{x\cos^{-1}x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx$

The left side is the exact differential of $xy$:

$d(xy) = \dfrac{x\cos^{-1}x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx$

Integrating both sides:

$xy = \int \dfrac{x\cos^{-1}x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx + C$

To evaluate the integral, use integration by parts. Let $u = \cos^{-1}x$ and $dv = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx$.

$du = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx$ and $v = -\sqrt{1-x^2}$

$\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$

$\int \dfrac{x\cos^{-1}x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx = -\sqrt{1-x^2}\cos^{-1}x - \int \left(-\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\right)\,dx$

$= -\sqrt{1-x^2}\cos^{-1}x - \int 1\,dx$

$= -\sqrt{1-x^2}\cos^{-1}x - x$

Substituting this back into the equation:

$xy = -\sqrt{1-x^2}\cos^{-1}x - x + C$

It is given that $\lim_{x\to 1^-} y(x) = 1$. Substituting $x = 1$ and $y = 1$:

$1(1) = -\sqrt{1-1^2}\cos^{-1}(1) - 1 + C$

$1 = 0 - 1 + C \Rightarrow C = 2$

The particular solution is:

$xy = 2 - x - \sqrt{1-x^2}\cos^{-1}x$

To find $y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, substitute $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$:

$\dfrac{1}{2}y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2} - \sqrt{1 - \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2}\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

$\dfrac{1}{2}y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{3}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$

$\dfrac{1}{2}y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{3}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt{3}}$

Multiplying by $2$:

$y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 3 - \dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$

questions.solution:
Given $cosx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 ) dy = ( 1 + ysinx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 ) ) dx$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{( 1 + ysinx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 ) )}{cosx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 )}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{cosx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 )} + \dfrac{ysinx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 ) )}{cosx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 )}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} - ( tanx ) y = \dfrac{1}{( 3sinx + cosx + 3 ) cosx}$

This is a linear differential equation of the type $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q,$ where $P = - tanx$ and $Q = \dfrac{1}{cosx\left(3sinx + cosx + 3\right)} .$

Now, the integrating factor $I . F . = {e}^{∫ Pdx} = {e}^{∫ - tanxdx}$

$= {e}^{ln\left|cosx\right|} = \left|cosx\right|$

$= cosx ∀ 0 \le x \le \dfrac{π}{2} .$

The solution of the given differential equation is $y\left(I . F .\right) = ∫ Q\left(I . F .\right)dx + C$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = ∫ ( cosx ) \cdot \dfrac{1}{cosx ( 3sinx + cosx + 3 )}dx + C$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = ∫ \dfrac{dx}{3sinx + cosx + 3}dx + C$

Using $sin2\theta = \dfrac{2tan\theta}{1 + {tan}^{2}\theta} \text{ and } cos2\theta = \dfrac{1 - {tan}^{2}\theta}{1 + {tan}^{2}\theta}$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = ∫ \dfrac{1}{3 \times \dfrac{2tan\dfrac{x}{2}}{1 + {tan}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}} + \dfrac{1 - {tan}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}}{1 + {tan}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}} + 3}dx + C$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = ∫ \dfrac{1 + {tan}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}}{6tan\dfrac{x}{2} + 1 - {tan}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2} + 3 + 3{tan}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}}dx + C$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = ∫ \left({sec}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}\right)2{tan}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2} + 6tan\dfrac{x}{2} + 4dx + C$

Let ${I}_{1} = ∫ \left({sec}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}\right)2\left({tan}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2} + 3tan\dfrac{x}{2} + 2\right)dx + C$

Put $tan\dfrac{x}{2} = t ⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}{sec}^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}dx = dt$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = ∫ \dfrac{dt}{{t}^{3} + 3t + 2} = ∫ \dfrac{dt}{\left(t + 2\right) ( t + 1 )}$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = ∫ \left(\dfrac{1}{t + 1} - \dfrac{1}{t + 2}\right)dt$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = {log}_{e}\left(t + 1\right) - {log}_{e}\left(t + 2\right)$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = {log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{t + 1}{t + 2}\right)$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = {log}_{e}\left|\left(\dfrac{tan\dfrac{x}{2} + 1}{tan\dfrac{x}{2} + 2}\right)\right|$

So, the solution is $y\left(cosx\right) = {log}_{e}\left|\dfrac{1 + tan\dfrac{x}{2}}{2 + tan\dfrac{x}{2}}\right| + C$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = {log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{1 + tan\dfrac{x}{2}}{2 + tan\dfrac{x}{2}}\right) + C$ for $0 \le x \le \dfrac{π}{2} .$

Now, it is given $y ( 0 ) = 0$

$⇒ 0 = {log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + C ⇒ C = {log}_{e}2$

$⇒ y\left(cosx\right) = {log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{1 + tan\dfrac{x}{2}}{2 + tan\dfrac{x}{2}}\right) + {log}_{e}2$

Now, for $x = \dfrac{π}{3},$ $y\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = {log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{3}}{2 + \dfrac{1}{3}}\right) + {log}_{e}2$

Given,

$\left(xcosx\right)dy + \left(xysinx + ycosx - 1\right)dx = 0$

$⇒ \left(xcosx\right)\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \left(yxsinx + ycosx\right) = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} + y\left(\dfrac{xsinx + cosx}{xcosx}\right) = \dfrac{1}{xcosx}$

Which is a linear differential equation of form $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + P\left(x\right)y = Q\left(x\right)$

Now we know that integrating factor will be ${e}^{∫ Pdx}$

$⇒ IF = {e}^{∫ \left(tanx + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx} = {e}^{ln\left|secx\right| + lnx} = x \cdot secx$

Hence, solution of linear differential equation is given by,

$⇒ y \cdot xsecx = ∫ \dfrac{xsecx}{xcosx}dx$

$⇒ xysecx = tanx + C$

Now using $\dfrac{π}{3}y\left(\dfrac{π}{3}\right) = \sqrt{3}$ we get,

$⇒ \dfrac{π}{3}y\left(\dfrac{π}{3}\right)sec\dfrac{π}{3} = tan\dfrac{π}{3} + C$

$⇒ C = \sqrt{3}$

Hence, $xysecx = tanx + \sqrt{3}$

$⇒ xy\left(x\right) = 2sin\left(x + \dfrac{π}{3}\right)$

Now differentiating both side we get,

$⇒ x{y}^{'}\left(x\right) + y\left(x\right) = 2cos\left(x + \dfrac{π}{3}\right)$

Now again differentiating we get,

$⇒ x{y}^{"} ( x ) + 2{y}^{'} ( x ) = - 2sin\left(x + \dfrac{π}{3}\right)$

Thus $\dfrac{π}{6}{y}^{"}\left(\dfrac{π}{6}\right) + 2{y}^{'}\left(\dfrac{π}{6}\right) = - 2$

$⇒ d\left(y \cdot ln\left(tan{x}^{2}\right)\right) - 4\sqrt{2}x\left(sin{x}^{2} - cos{x}^{2}\right)\sqrt{2}\left(2sin{x}^{2}cos{x}^{2}\right)dx = 0$

$⇒ d\left(yln\left(tan{x}^{2}\right)\right) - \dfrac{4x\left(sin{x}^{2} - cos{x}^{2}\right)}{\left(sin{x}^{2} + {cos}^{2}x\right)2 - 1}dx = 0$

$⇒ yln\left(tan{x}^{2}\right) + 2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}ln\left|\dfrac{t - 1}{t + 1}\right| = c$

$⇒ y = - 1$

Given differential equation is $2\left({x}^{2} + {x}^{5 / 4}\right)dy - y\left(x + {x}^{1 / 4}\right)dx = 2{x}^{9 / 4}dx$

$⇒ 2\left({x}^{2} + {x}^{5 / 4}\right)\dfrac{dy}{dx} - y\left(x + {x}^{1 / 4}\right) = 2{x}^{9 / 4}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} - \dfrac{y\left(x + {x}^{1 / 4}\right)}{2\left({x}^{2} + {x}^{5 / 4}\right)} = \dfrac{2{x}^{9 / 4}}{2\left({x}^{2} + {x}^{5 / 4}\right)}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} - \dfrac{y\left(x + {x}^{1 / 4}\right)}{2x\left(x + {x}^{1 / 4}\right)} = \dfrac{2{x}^{9 / 4}}{2{x}^{5 / 4}\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right)}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} - \dfrac{y}{2x} = x\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right)$

This is a linear differential equation of the type $\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q,$ where $P = - \dfrac{1}{2x}$ and $Q = \dfrac{x}{{x}^{3 / 4} + 1}$

Now, we have integrating factor $I . F . = {e}^{∫ Pdx}$

$= {e}^{- ∫ \dfrac{dx}{2x}} = {e}^{- \dfrac{1}{2}{log}_{e}x}$

$= {e}^{{log}_{e}{x}^{- \dfrac{1}{2}}} = {x}^{- \dfrac{1}{2}}$

Now, the solution of the linear differential equation is $y \times \left(I . F .\right) = ∫ Q \times \left(I . F .\right)dx + C$

$⇒ y \cdot {x}^{- 1 / 2} = ∫ x \cdot {x}^{- 1 / 2}\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right)dx + C$

$⇒ y \cdot {x}^{- 1 / 2} = ∫ {x}^{1 / 2}\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right)dx + C$

$⇒ y \cdot {x}^{- 1 / 2} = 4 ∫ {t}^{2}dt - 4 ∫ \dfrac{t2}{{t}^{3} + 1}dt + C$

$⇒ y \cdot {x}^{- 1 / 2} = \dfrac{4{t}^{3}}{3} - \dfrac{4}{3}{log}_{e}\left({t}^{3} + 1\right) + C$

$⇒ y \cdot {x}^{- 1 / 2} = \dfrac{4{x}^{3 / 4}}{3} - \dfrac{4}{3}{log}_{e}\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right) + C$

Now, the curve passes through $\left(1, 1 - \dfrac{4}{3}{log}_{e}2\right)$

$⇒ 1 - \dfrac{4}{3}{log}_{e}2 = \dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac{4}{3}{log}_{e}2 + C$

$⇒ C = - \dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ y \cdot {x}^{- 1 / 2} = \dfrac{4}{3}{x}^{3 / 4} - \dfrac{4}{3}{log}_{e}\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right) - \dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ y = \dfrac{4}{3}{x}^{5 / 4} - \dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt{x}{log}_{e}\left({x}^{3 / 4} + 1\right) - \dfrac{x}{3}$

Hence, at $x = 16,$ we get

$⇒ y\left(16\right) = 4\left(\dfrac{31}{3} - \dfrac{8}{3}{log}_{e}3\right) .$

If p and q are respectively the points of local minima and local maxima of g, then the value of $|\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{q}|$ is equal to $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
Given $f(x) = 1 - 2x + \int_0^x e^{(x-t)} f(t) \, dt$.
Differentiating and simplifying:
$e^{-x}f'(x) - e^{-x}f(x) = -2e^{-x} + (1-2x)e^{-x}(-1) + e^{-x}f(x)$
This reduces to:
$f'(x) - 2f(x) = 2x - 3$
Solving the linear ODE $\frac{dy}{dx} - 2y = 2x - 3$:
$y \cdot e^{-2x} = \int e^{-2x}(2x-3)\,dx$
On solving, we get $f(x) = 1 - x$.
Now, $g(x) = \int_0^x (3-t)^{15}(t-4)^6(t+12)^{17} \, dt$
$g'(x) = (3-x)^{15}(x-4)^6(x+12)^{17}$
$= -(x-3)^{15}(x-4)^6(x+12)^{17}$
Sign analysis of $g'(x)$:
$g'(x) $changes from $+ \to - $at $x = 3 $→ local maxima $(q = 3)$
$g'(x) $changes from $- \to + $at $x = -12 $→ local minima $(p = -12)$
$|p + q| = |-12 + 3| = 9$

questions.solution:
Given,

$F\left(x\right) = {e}^{- x}{∫}_{3}^{x}\left(3{t}^{2} + 2t + 4{F}^{'}\left(t\right)\right)dt .$

So, $F\left(3\right) = {e}^{- 3}{∫}_{3}^{3}\left(3{t}^{2} + 2t + 4{F}^{'}\left(t\right)\right)dt .$

$⇒ F\left(3\right) = 0$

Again, ${e}^{x}F\left(x\right) = {∫}_{3}^{x}\left(3{t}^{2} + 2t + 4{F}^{'}\left(t\right)\right)dt$

Differentiate both sides

$⇒ {e}^{x}F\left(x\right) + {e}^{x}{F}^{'}\left(x\right) = 3{x}^{2} + 2x + 4{F}^{'}\left(x\right)$ (Newton Leibnitz Theorem for Definite Integral)

$⇒ \left({e}^{x} - 4\right)\dfrac{dy}{dx} + {e}^{x}y = \left(3{x}^{2} + 2x\right)$ (Use $y = F\left(x\right)$)

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} + {e}^{x}\left({e}^{x} - 4\right)y = \left(3{x}^{2} + 2x\right)\left({e}^{x} - 4\right)$

Here, integrating factor is ${e}^{∫ \dfrac{ex}{{e}^{x} - 4}dx} = {e}^{ln\left({e}^{x} - 4\right)} = {e}^{x} - 4$

So, the solution is

$y \cdot \left({e}^{x} - 4\right) = ∫ \left(3{x}^{2} + 2x\right)dx + c$

$⇒ y \cdot \left({e}^{x} - 4\right) = \left({x}^{3} + {x}^{2}\right) + c$

Put $x = 3, y = 0 ⇒ c = - 36$

So, $F\left(x\right) = \left({x}^{3} + {x}^{2} - 36\right)\left({e}^{x} - 4\right)$

So, $\alpha = 12 \text{ and } \beta = 4$

Hence, $\alpha + \beta = 16$

$⇒ \dfrac{dt}{dx} = 2x{t}^{3} - xt$

$⇒ \dfrac{dt}{dx} + xt = 2x{t}^{3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{t3}\dfrac{dt}{dx} + \dfrac{x}{t2} = 2x . . . \left(i\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{- 2}{t3}\dfrac{dt}{dx} = \dfrac{du}{dx}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{t3}\dfrac{dt}{dx} = \dfrac{- 1}{2}\dfrac{du}{dx}$

$⇒ \dfrac{e- {x}^{2}}{t2} = ∫ {e}^{- {x}^{2}}\left(- 4x\right)dx$

Let ${e}^{y} = t ⇒ {e}^{y}\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dt}{dx}$

So,
